questiontext.text:
What is the value of t after running these statements?

t = [1, 2, 3]
t.pop(1)
t.append(2)
t.remove(3)

feedback.text: t.pop(1) removes the second element, which is 2.
After t.pop(1) removes the second element, t.append(2) adds 2 to the end of the list, and t.remove(3) removes 3.

What is the value of b after running these statements?

b = a
a.remove(2)

feedback.text: a.remove(2) removes the value 2 from the list.

questiontext.text:
What can we say about two lists created like this:

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]

feedback.text: a and b refer to different lists, so they are not identical.

answer.text: They are identical but not equivalent.

questiontext.text: Having more than one name for the same object can lead to subtle bugs, but it is relatively safe with strings. Why?

answer.text: Assigning a string to another variable makes a copy, so the two variables never refer to the same string.

feedback.text: Assignment doesn't copy: after b = a, a and b refer to the same string, and b is a is True.

answer.text: Two strings with the same letters are never identical.

feedback.text: In the chapter's example, a = 'banana' and b = 'banana' create only one string, so a is b is True.

answer.text: The is operator doesn't work with strings.

feedback.text: The is operator works with any objects, including strings.

answer.text: Strings are immutable, so nothing can change the string through one name and surprise the other.

feedback.text: Strings are immutable, so a string that has two names can't be changed through either one.
